tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

Why must the sweep eventually terminate?
The fixed scenario performs finitely many allocations, so eventually n is larger than all of them.

## Notes/Tips from Spec
Mutation 3 asks for a tree of a million
nodes, and valgrind runs many times slower than native. Put the million-node case behind a flag
or its own target so make memcheck still finishes inside a coffee break: run the large case under
asan, which is fast enough, and a smaller case under valgrind. What you must not do is quietly
shrink the large case because a timing problem was inconvenient. If your harness ends up running
the “million-node” teardown at ten thousand nodes, say so in REFLECTION.md, and expect the
walkthrough to ask about it.

## Thresholds
4096-byte slabs. O(1)
for pool_alloc and
pool_free. 106 nodes
under a 64 KB stack. live
+ free_objs == slabs *
objs_per_slab. Zero leaks,
not few.
## Choices left up to me
Where the slab header lives.
What alignment you guarantee and how the stride enforces it. Right-spine teardown or pointer reversal? Morris or parent pointers? What
your rb_foreach contract 
says about callbacks that call
back in?
DECIDED (2026-10-06, Mutation 2 pool design — recorded before any `src/pool.c` code exists):

**1. Alignment.** Slots are aligned to `_Alignof(max_align_t)` (fundamental alignment). The
slot stride is `obj_size` rounded up to that alignment, and is also never smaller than
`sizeof(void *)` so a dead slot can hold the intrusive free-list `next`. Because the first
slot's offset inside the slab and the stride are both multiples of that alignment, and the
block `rb_malloc` returns is already `max_align_t`-aligned, *every* slot address
(`base + start + i*stride`) is aligned — not just slot 0. Getting only slot 0 right is the
version of this bug that works and then works less.

Why: `pool_create(size_t obj_size)` takes no alignment parameter, so the pool cannot be told
what its caller needs and has to promise one unilaterally. The conservative fundamental
promise costs some internal padding when `obj_size` is not already a multiple of it — for the
current ~48-byte `struct rb_node` that cost happens to be zero, which is an accident worth
noticing and not relying on — and buys a guarantee that stays true if the node layout changes.
It also satisfies both uses a slot's bytes are put to across its lifetime: the live object
while it is live, and the free-list pointer written over its front when it dies. The spec
flags this as a `-fsanitize=undefined` matter ("alignment is one of those requirements that
feels ceremonial until it is wrong"), and `make asan` is a gate, so a misalignment here is a
build failure rather than a mystery.

LIMIT (explicit): `max_align_t` is a *fundamental*-alignment guarantee only. It is not support
for over-aligned types — anything demanding more than `max_align_t` via `_Alignas` (a
cache-line-aligned or over-aligned SIMD object, say) is outside this pool's contract and would
need an alignment parameter the frozen API does not have.

**2. Slab metadata: in-band**, at the front of each 4096-byte slab.

Why: one `rb_malloc` per slab, and therefore exactly one failure point when the pool grows.
Out-of-band metadata would add a second allocation per slab, which means a second failure path
with a real unwind (slab bought, header allocation fails => release the slab and leave the
pool's counters untouched) and a second object for `pool_destroy` to release. In-band trades
payload space to keep the pool's only failure mode "buy a new slab."

Cost accepted: usable space is `4096 - header - alignment padding`, not 4096, so
`objs_per_slab` must be derived from what is left after the header. That is precisely the
off-by-one Figure 4's caption warns about ("the slab header, which eats bytes the naive
division forgets") and that the spec's own adversarial-review prompt for M2 tells the reviewer
to hunt for, alongside the tail slack that must never be handed out.

Consequence for teardown: the next-slab link lives *inside* the block being released, so
`pool_destroy` must read `next` before `rb_free`ing that slab — the same "save the pointer
before you free the thing that contains it" rule as the HW1 right-spine teardown, one level
down.

Not relied on: the spec notes that in-band metadata makes "which slab is this object in?"
answerable by masking. That requires page-*aligned* slabs, and `rb_malloc` forwards to
`malloc`, which guarantees `max_align_t` (16 bytes), not 4096 — so masking is not actually
available here and forms no part of this justification. Nothing in this design needs the
object->slab mapping anyway: a single intrusive free list makes `pool_free` indifferent to
which slab an object came from, which is what keeps it O(1).

**3. `pool_stats` / `free_objs`:** the spec's operational definition — every slot that already
exists which `pool_alloc` could return without calling `rb_malloc` again. That is free-list
slots **plus** uncarved capacity in slabs already bought, because `pool_alloc` satisfies both
without allocating and the caller cannot tell which path a slot arrived by. Hence
`live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`.

What that invariant actually asserts: every slot that exists is in exactly one of three states
— live, on the free list, or never yet carved — with the last two both counting as
`free_objs`, and none lost or double-counted. Tail slack is not a slot and contributes to
neither side. It therefore catches a slot dropped on the floor, a slot handed out twice, a
double `pool_free` (which also makes the free list cyclic), a carve loop that steps one slot
into the slack, and a slab counted before its allocation actually succeeded — including after
an injected failure, when it must still hold. Per the spec it is asserted repeatedly while the
allocator is under stress, not once at the end: "the earliest assertion failure is usually much
more informative than the corpse you discover ten thousand operations later."

Still open (deliberately not decided yet): whether the three numbers come from maintained
counters, an on-demand walk of the free list, or counters plus a debug-only walk that
cross-checks them; how the tests get at `objs_per_slab`, given the public API does not expose
it and having the tests recompute it would let a geometry bug cancel out of its own check;
whether `pool_stats` tolerates NULL out-parameters; whether `pool_create` buys a slab eagerly
or lazily; and what a `obj_size` too large to fit even once should do.


## Confusions
“Why does pool reuse hide useafter-free from ASan?” “What
exactly happens between the
node alloc and the key copy?”
“Why can’t the teardown loop
spin forever?”

content.text:
Inspection complete. Here's what's there and the plan.

## Inspection findings

**`struct rbtree`** (`src/rbtree.c:19`) — 3 fields: `root`, `size`, `value_free`. No allocator state at all.

**Node-storage call sites — exactly four:**
| site | current call |
|---|---|
| `rb_insert` (`:124`) | `rb_malloc(sizeof *n)` |
| `rb_insert` key-copy failure (`:129`) | `rb_free(n)` |
| `rb_delete` (`:277`) | `rb_free(n)` |
| `rb_destroy` (`:420`) | `rb_free(cur)` |

**Key-copy sites (must stay `rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, variable length):** insert `:127`, delete `:250`/`:273`, destroy `:417`. **Tree handle:** `rb_create` `:29`, `rb_destroy` `:429`.

**`src/pool.c`** exports `rb_pool_geometry`, `pool_create`, `pool_alloc`, `pool_free`, `pool_stats`, `pool_destroy` with external linkage and no header (deliberate — fixed file map). `rb_pool_t` is file-private and incomplete elsewhere. `pool_create(obj_size)` is lazy (1 `rb_malloc`), `pool_alloc` costs 1 `rb_malloc` only when it must grow, `pool_free` poisons the full stride with `0xDD` in debug builds, `pool_destroy` tolerates live objects.

**Tests:** `rb_create(...)` appears at ~30 sites, all in `static void test_*` / `run_delete_case` / `build_seven_key_fixture`. `check()` is a single file-scope reporter. Fault tests `test_fault_rb_create_failure`/`_insert_node_alloc_failure`/`_insert_key_alloc_failure` hardcode `n` = 1/2/3; `test_fault_sweep` is already ordinal-free (arms `n`, asserts `fault_alloc_total() == n` *at* the observed failure, terminates on `total < n`). `tests/fuzz.c` calls `rb_create(NULL)` once, at `:88`; argv is `ops [seed]`.

---

## Plan

### A. Minimum state on `struct rbtree`

One field:

```c
struct rbtree {
    struct rb_node   *root;
    size_t            size;
    rb_value_free_fn  value_free;
    rb_pool_t        *pool;   /* NULL => ordinary rb_malloc node storage */
};
```

`NULL` *is* the mode discriminator — no enum, no flag, no second struct. `rb_create` sets it to `NULL`; `rb_create_pooled` sets it to a live pool. `rbtree.c` gets a top-of-file `extern` block for the four pool entry points plus `typedef struct rb_pool rb_pool_t;` left **incomplete**, exactly as `tests/test_rbtree.c:36-42` already does — no `src/pool.h`, and no pool layout visible to tree logic.

The tree handle itself stays `rb_malloc` in both modes; the pool's `obj_size` is `sizeof(struct rb_node)` and nothing else is drawn from it.

### B. Centralization — yes, two helpers, zero mode branches outside them

```c
static struct rb_node *node_alloc(rbtree_t *t) {
    return t->pool ? pool_alloc(t->pool) : rb_malloc(sizeof(struct rb_node));
}
static void node_release(rbtree_t *t, struct rb_node *n) {
    if (t->pool) pool_free(t->pool, n); else rb_free(n);
}
```

That turns the four sites above into `node_alloc(t)` / `node_release(t, n)` and is the entire change to insert/delete/destroy. `rb_create_pooled` is then three lines:

```c
rbtree_t *rb_create_pooled(rb_value_free_fn value_free) {
    rbtree_t *t = rb_create(value_free);          /* also sets t->pool = NULL */
    if (t == NULL) return NULL;
    t->pool = pool_create(sizeof(struct rb_node));
    if (t->pool == NULL) { rb_free(t); return NULL; }
    return t;
}
```

No `goto` needed — one resource held at the single failure point. Diff to `rbtree.c`: ~20 lines added, 4 lines changed.

### C. Ownership / failure paths

| failure | what is freed | who owns `value` |
|---|---|---|
| `rb_create_pooled`: tree-handle `rb_malloc` fails | nothing — pool not yet created (allocation order is tree-then-pool precisely so this path has nothing to unwind) | n/a; returns `NULL` |
| `rb_create_pooled`: `pool_create` fails | `rb_free(t)` only. `pool_create` is itself all-or-nothing (geometry checked before its single `rb_malloc`), so there is no half-built pool | n/a; returns `NULL` |
| `rb_insert`: `pool_alloc` fails (grow failed) | nothing. `pool_grow` mutates no counter on failure and `pool_alloc` touches none before it, so the pool is bit-identical; tree untouched (both fallible steps precede the first pointer write) | **caller**. Return `-1` |
| `rb_insert`: key copy fails after `pool_alloc` succeeded | `node_release(t, n)` → `pool_free(pool, n)`. The slot returns to the free list (and is poisoned), `live` goes back down, so `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab` still holds. `n->value` was never assigned | **caller**. Return `-1` |

In all four the tree's observable state (`rb_size`, `rb_find`, `rb_validate`) is identical to before the call, and `value_free` is never invoked.

### D. Delete

`rb_delete`'s only change is `rb_free(n)` → `node_release(t, n)`. It still performs **no allocation**: `pool_free` is a poison-memset plus a link write plus two counter updates, and `rb_free` is `free`. `test_fault_delete_allocates_nothing` and the sweep's `delete performed no allocation in-scenario` assertion therefore stay true verbatim in pooled mode — worth re-running rather than rewriting.

### E. `rb_destroy` ordering

Required order, per node, then once at the end:

1. **Capture `next`** from `cur->left`/`cur->right` — before anything is released. Already correct in the existing loop, and now load-bearing twice over: `pool_free` memsets the whole stride to `0xDD`, so a `next` read after release would be a dereference of `0xDDDD…`, which (unlike `rb_free`) ASan cannot see because the slab is still live memory.
2. `rb_free(cur->key)` — key lives outside the pool; must happen while `cur` is still readable.
3. `t->value_free(cur->value)` — same reason.
4. `node_release(t, cur)` — pooled: slot to the free list; ordinary: `rb_free`.
5. After the walk terminates: `if (t->pool) pool_destroy(t->pool);` then `rb_free(t)`.

`pool_destroy` must be last because every node the walk traverses physically lives inside a slab it releases. Keys and values are *not* in slabs, so steps 2–3 cannot be skipped in favour of letting `pool_destroy` reclaim everything — that is the leak this ordering exists to prevent.

Note on step 4: going through `node_release` per node rather than letting `pool_destroy` reclaim node storage wholesale costs an O(n) walk we are already doing, and buys an assertable end state (`live == 0` just before `pool_destroy`), which is a direct test for "no node dropped on the floor by teardown." I'd take that.

### F. Running the A1 + M1 battery on both trees

Parameterize the factory, don't duplicate the suite:

```c
typedef rbtree_t *(*tree_factory_fn)(rb_value_free_fn);
static tree_factory_fn make_tree  = rb_create;
static const char     *mode_label = "heap";
```

Then `sed` all ~30 `rb_create(` → `make_tree(` **inside the `test_*` bodies only** (the fault tests that name `rb_create` as the thing under test keep it; see G), prefix `mode_label` in `check()`'s printf so a failure names its mode, and in `main()` lift the existing A1/M1 call list into `static void run_tree_suite(void)` invoked twice:

```c
make_tree = rb_create;         mode_label = "heap";   run_tree_suite();
make_tree = rb_create_pooled;  mode_label = "pooled"; run_tree_suite();
```

Cost: one typedef, one one-line change to `check`, a mechanical identifier swap, and `main()` restructured. No test logic is copied, weakened, or skipped. Pool-internal tests (`test_pool_*`, geometry) stay out of `run_tree_suite` — they are not tree tests.

For the fuzzer: accept `argv[3]` as a mode selector at `fuzz.c:88` and run it twice from the Makefile's `test` target (and `memcheck`, which doubles valgrind time — flag that in the commit message rather than quietly shrinking the op count).

One caveat to record, not to fix: pool slot reuse means a pooled-mode use-after-free lands in live slab memory and ASan stays silent (NOTES.md's own "Confusions" names this). The pooled pass is strictly weaker at UAF detection, so ordinary mode remains the primary sanitizer target and the `0xDD` poison is what does the work in pooled mode.

### G. Fault-sweep ordinals — what shifts, and no hardcoded `n`

What changes under pooled node storage:

- **Creation is 2 `rb_malloc` calls, not 1** (tree handle, then pool struct). So `n=1` and `n=2` both make creation return `NULL`, via two *different* unwind paths — both worth arming.
- **Insert's node allocation is no longer one `rb_malloc` per insert.** `pool_alloc` hits `rb_malloc` only on a grow: once for the first insert, then once per `objs_per_slab` nodes, and **zero** times whenever the free list is non-empty. So the first insert costs 2 (slab + key copy), subsequent inserts in the same slab cost 1 (key copy only), and an insert reusing a freed slot costs 1.
- **Key copy is still exactly one `rb_malloc` per new-key insert** — unchanged, and now the *only* guaranteed allocation in an insert.
- **Overwrite, delete, destroy, `pool_free`: still zero.** Unchanged.

So the hardcoded `fault_alloc_arm(1/2/3)` in `test_fault_rb_create_failure`, `_insert_node_alloc_failure`, `_insert_key_alloc_failure` are statements about `rbtree.c`'s own ordinals and should stay ordinary-mode-only. The pooled analogues use **discover-then-arm**: run the scenario once with the injector disarmed, record `fault_alloc_total()` at the point of interest, then re-run arming that *discovered* ordinal. No literal `n` anywhere.

`test_fault_sweep` needs no ordinal change at all — it arms an unbounded sequence of `n`, asserts `fault_alloc_total() == n` at whatever call actually failed, and terminates on `total < n`. That structure is already mode-agnostic. The two things it needs are (a) creation failure handled for a 2-call create (its `if (t == NULL)` branch currently asserts `total == n` which stays correct, but the comment "rb_create's own allocation" becomes wrong), and (b) its per-insert assertions stated as *observed deltas* rather than counts — `delta ∈ {1, 2}` for a successful new-key insert, `0` for overwrite and delete.

**Optional but cheap and I'd recommend it:** an `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS`-gated `rb_test_pool_stats(const rbtree_t *t, size_t *slabs, size_t *live, size_t *free_objs)` in `rbtree.c`, so the pooled pass can assert `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab` *and* `live == rb_size(t)` after real insert/delete workloads — right now that invariant is only checkable against a standalone pool, never against one a tree is actually driving.

---

### Commit slicing (3 commits, all from green)

1. `M2: struct rbtree pool field + node_alloc/node_release + rb_create_pooled` — `src/rbtree.c` only; suite still runs heap-only, must stay green with zero behavioral change.
2. `M2: run the A1+M1 suite and fuzzer against both tree factories` — `tests/test_rbtree.c`, `tests/fuzz.c`, `Makefile`.
3. `M2: pooled fault paths via discover-then-arm + tree-driven pool invariant` — new pooled fault tests and the stats hook.

Nothing touches `include/rbtree.h`. Nothing touches `rb_snapshot`, `rb_foreach`, or Mutation 3.

**Open question I'd like your call on before I start:** whether commit 2 should double the `memcheck` fuzz invocation (2 × 20000 ops under valgrind, roughly doubling that target's runtime) or run the pooled fuzz pass under asan only, with valgrind staying heap-only. I lean toward doubling it and keeping both honest — but it's your coffee break.

Awaiting approval.

79	 * to unwind: the handle first (nothing held if it fails), then the pool

81	 * it validates the geometry before its single rb_malloc -- so there is never

content.text:
Diff is above (97 insertions, 4 changed lines, `src/rbtree.c` only). Here's the battery and the spec comparison.

## Battery — all green from a clean rebuild

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `make test` | All tests passed; fuzz 100000 ops OK |
| `make asan` (`-fsanitize=address,undefined`, clean rebuild) | All tests passed; fuzz 100000 ops OK; zero findings |
| `make memcheck` | `test_rbtree`: ERROR SUMMARY 0 errors, "All heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible"; `fuzz 20000`: same |

The committed suite does not reach `rb_create_pooled` yet — that's slice 2 — so slice 1 would otherwise ship unexercised. I wrote a throwaway driver in the scratchpad (`pooled_smoke.c`, **not** added to the repo) to verify the pooled path before committing. 25 checks, all passing, and clean under both tools:

- 300 pooled inserts (4 slabs), validate, find; delete 150 (exercises `pool_free` via `node_release`), validate, `value_free` called exactly 150×; reinsert 150 into the freed slots, validate; `rb_destroy` with 300 **live** nodes → `value_free` called exactly 300×.
- `rb_destroy` of an empty pooled tree, where the lazy pool never bought a slab.
- `rb_create_pooled` both failure paths: armed at call 1 (handle) → NULL; armed at call 2 (`pool_create`) → NULL with the handle released.
- Pooled create costs exactly 2 `rb_malloc` calls (measured, not assumed). Key-copy failure armed at the 2nd call *of the insert* → lands on the key copy, not the slab grow; returns `-1`; tree unchanged; `value_free` never ran; and the next insert costs **1** `rb_malloc` (key only), proving the rolled-back slot was reused rather than stranded.
- Pooled `rb_delete` with the next allocation armed: succeeds, `fault_alloc_total() == 0`.

`pooled_smoke` under asan/ubsan: exit 0, zero findings. Under valgrind: "All heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible", 0 errors.

## Current implementation vs. what the spec expects

**Met:**
- `rb_create_pooled` exists and draws *node* storage from the internal slab pool; `sizeof(struct rb_node)` is still 48, so `tests/test_rbtree.c:1019`'s "48 is … what `rb_create_pooled` will ask for" is now a true statement rather than a prediction.
- All heap allocation in `src/` still routes through the seam — `pool.c` itself calls `rb_malloc` for slabs and the pool struct, so the pooled tree is fully fault-injectable. No direct `malloc`/`free` anywhere in `src/`.
- Variable-length key copies stay on `rb_malloc`/`rb_free`, as required — a fixed-stride pool cannot hold them.
- Every allocation checked; both `rb_create_pooled` failure paths and the insert rollback leave state unchanged, return the documented code, and leave `value` caller-owned.
- 4096-byte slabs, O(1) `pool_alloc`/`pool_free`, zero leaks. `include/rbtree.h` untouched. No `src/pool.h` — file map unchanged.
- Smallest diff that works: one struct field, two helpers, four call sites, one teardown branch. No unrelated refactoring, no `goto` (one resource at the single failure point doesn't warrant the ladder).

**Deliberate gaps, flagged not hidden:**
1. **The graded suite still never constructs a pooled tree.** Slice 1's evidence is a scratch driver. Slice 2 is what makes it a deliverable; until then the repo's own tests prove only *no regression*.
2. **`live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab` is never checked against a tree-driven pool.** Per your revision 1, pooled teardown doesn't walk `live` down to zero, and per revision 4 there's no `rb_test_pool_stats` hook, so a node the teardown walk skipped is caught by valgrind on its *leaked key*, not by the pool invariant. That's adequate — a skipped node always leaks a key — but it is indirect, and it's the reason I'd keep an eye on the existing tests' sufficiency as slice 2 lands.
3. **Pooled mode is strictly weaker for use-after-free.** A freed node's slot stays live slab memory, so ASan is silent; only the `0xDD` poison catches it. This is NOTES.md's own "Confusions" item, now a real property of the integration. Ordinary mode remains the primary sanitizer target.
4. `rb_snapshot` is declared and undefined (M4). Links fine because nothing calls it. Out of scope, as agreed, and Mutation 3 untouched.

**One thing I'd correct in my own plan:** I claimed `rb_destroy` would assert `live == 0` before `pool_destroy`. Your revision removes that, and you're right that it was buying little for an O(n) poisoning pass — but gap 2 above is the honest price, so I'd rather name it than let the plan's old justification stand unamended.

Ready to commit as `M2: pooled node storage — rb_create_pooled, node_alloc/node_release, teardown mode handling`. Say go and I'll commit; nothing is staged yet.

## What changed

**`tests/test_rbtree.c`** — factory indirection, not a mechanical sweep:
- `typedef rbtree_t *(*tree_factory_fn)(rb_value_free_fn); static tree_factory_fn make_tree = rb_create;` plus a `mode_label` that `check()` prefixes, so a failure names its mode instead of leaving two identical descriptions ambiguous.
- 29 of 32 `rb_create` sites → `make_tree`. **Three deliberately kept:** `test_fault_rb_create_failure`, `_insert_node_alloc_failure`, `_insert_key_alloc_failure`. Their subject *is* `rbtree.c`'s ordinals (1 = handle, 2 = node struct, 3 = key copy); under the pool those are different allocations in different numbers, so a pooled run of them would not be the same claim.
- `main()` split into `run_tree_suite()` + two passes. The suite includes `test_fault_overwrite_allocates_nothing`, `test_fault_delete_allocates_nothing` and **the full sweep** — all three claims are allocator-independent.
- The sweep is structurally untouched: still the natural `n = 1, 2, 3, …` loop, still `fault_alloc_total() == n`, still terminating on `total < n`. The only edit is one **message** reword (`"rb_create's own allocation was the n-th call"` → `"tree creation failed at the armed call n"`), because under the pool creation spans two allocations so `n == 1` and `n == 2` both land there. No assertion changed.
- Three new pooled targeted tests for the claims the heap tests can't make: both creation unwind paths, slab-purchase failure, and key-copy failure — the last asserting the follow-up insert costs exactly **1** `rb_malloc`, which proves the rolled-back slot was returned to the pool rather than stranded.
- One message fix: `"rb_create returns non-NULL"` → `"tree factory returns non-NULL"` (line 77 was the only suite description naming a constructor).

**`tests/fuzz.c`** — `fuzz <ops> [seed|-] [heap|pooled]`. `-` preserves `time(NULL)` seeding so both passes keep exploring new op streams. Unknown mode is a hard error.

**`Makefile`** — `test` runs the fuzzer at the **full 100000** in both modes; `memcheck` runs 20000 in both modes under valgrind. Op counts unreduced; that's three valgrind invocations now.

## Battery

| gate | result |
|---|---|
| `make test` | 1897 assertions, **0 failures**; fuzz heap 100000 OK; fuzz pooled 100000 OK |
| `make asan` (clean rebuild, address+UB) | all passed, both fuzz modes, zero findings |

**Coverage proof, since "it passed" isn't evidence the second pass ran:** heap emitted 637 labelled assertions, pooled 613. Diffing the two description sets with the sweep excluded: **identical — all 565 non-sweep tree assertions ran in both modes, same descriptions, same order.** No test silently degraded into a no-op.

The 24-assertion delta is entirely sweep arithmetic, and I checked it rather than assuming:
- **Sweep iterations: heap 8, pooled 7.** Heap allocates 1 (create) + 3 × 2 (inserts) = 7, so it terminates at `n = 8`. Pooled allocates 2 (handle + pool) + 2 (slab + key) + 1 + 1 = 6, terminating at `n = 7`.
- **The 5 "test fixture malloc succeeded" lines** are `make_int` calls from *inside* the sweep, which my first grep misfiled as non-sweep. Hand-derived per iteration: heap 0+1+1+2+2+3+3+4 = 16, pooled 0+0+1+1+2+3+4 = 11. Difference 5, matching exactly.

DID: re-read the Mutation 2 material end to end rather than working from the summary — §8's preamble on the three accumulating contracts, the companion discussion of per-allocation overhead and slabs (pp. 10–11, incl. the `kmem_cache`/Solaris lineage), §8.2's API and constraints, Figure 4 and its caption, the "what still comes from `rb_malloc`" paragraph, the ASan/poisoning discussion, the M2 rubric row, and the spec's own adversarial-review prompt for M2. Worked through what an `rb_pool_t` owns (slabs, a carve cursor, a free-list head), the three states a slot can be in (live / free-listed / uncarved), why the intrusive `next` may legally live in a dead object's own bytes (the slot is dead, big enough, and — given the stride — aligned enough), why `pool_alloc`/`pool_free` are O(1) (all deciding happened at `pool_create`; no size search, no coalescing, and no object->slab lookup on the hot path), and why `pool_destroy` can release whole slabs with live objects in them (the pool owns slabs, not objects). Then laid out the three decisions the spec leaves open, with tradeoffs and failure paths for each, and did not choose.
DECIDED: (1) slots are aligned to `_Alignof(max_align_t)`, with the stride `obj_size` rounded up to that alignment and never below `sizeof(void *)`, so every slot address is aligned rather than only slot 0 — the pool cannot be told its caller's alignment (`pool_create` takes only `obj_size`), so it promises one conservatively; noted explicitly that this is fundamental alignment and NOT support for over-aligned (`_Alignas`-beyond-`max_align_t`) types. (2) slab metadata lives in-band at the front of each slab, accepting the payload cost and the "header eats bytes the naive division forgets" off-by-one in exchange for one `rb_malloc` per slab and therefore one failure point when the pool grows, instead of out-of-band's second allocation with its own unwind path. (3) `free_objs` follows the spec's operational definition — free-list slots plus uncarved capacity in existing slabs — giving `live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab`. Full reasoning, costs accepted, and consequences recorded in NOTES.md under HW2 "Choices left up to me".
LEARNED: the two layers of Figure 4 are the useful separation — slab layout answers "where is the storage?" and is fixed arithmetic, while free-list policy answers "which slot next?" and ignores physical layout entirely; keeping them apart means geometry and history can be tested independently. Also that "pooled tree" does not mean "no ordinary allocation": nodes come from the pool, but key copies stay variable-length and keep coming from `rb_malloc`, which is why pooled teardown can return node storage wholesale yet still has to visit every node. And that the spec's in-band selling point of answering "which slab is this?" by masking does not actually hold here, because `rb_malloc` forwards to `malloc` and guarantees `max_align_t` alignment, not page alignment — so that benefit was excluded from the justification rather than claimed.

The spec's file-level map (§7) names only `src/pool.c`, and the repo already has the `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` precedent for test-only visibility into internals, so the geometry type and helper stay inside `src/pool.c` and the test declares the helper itself. Out-parameters instead of a shared geometry struct follow directly: with no header, a struct would have to be duplicated in the test, and a duplicated layout is a real hazard for no benefit. The helper has external linkage rather than `static` specifically so the production build (where no `pool_create` calls it yet) stays clean under `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` without broadening `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` or adding build machinery — a `static` unused function would have been a `-Wunused-function` error. (2) internal degenerate-size contract: `obj_size == 0` returns false, any size for which no complete slot fits returns false, the oversize check runs *before* the alignment rounding so the arithmetic can never wrap (hence `SIZE_MAX` returns false rather than reporting capacity that does not exist), and the output geometry is zeroed on every false return. This is explicitly an internal contract — what `pool_create` should do with a rejected `obj_size` stays a later decision. (3) the direct test asserts the partition as `slot0_offset + objs_per_slab*stride + slack == 4096`, and tests minimal padding without overflow via `effective_min = max(obj_size, sizeof(void *))`, `stride >= effective_min`, `stride - effective_min < ALIGN`. ## 2026-10-08 (HW2 Mutation 2 / M2 slice 2, planned as "slice A" — pool lifecycle, ~1.5h)
STATE: the geometry slice is green and committed (`febfdc2`); `src/pool.c` held `rb_pool_geometry` and the in-band `struct rb_slab` and nothing else. The four questions the previous evening left open (counter strategy, eager vs. lazy first slab, NULL tolerance in `pool_stats`, what `pool_create` does with a rejected `obj_size`) were all answered before any code was written, because every one of them shapes the struct.
IMPLEMENTED NOW (slice A): `struct rb_pool` with its full field set, `pool_create`, `pool_stats`, `pool_destroy`. `pool_create` computes the geometry *before* allocating and caches all four numbers, so it has exactly one fallible step and no unwind path; a rejected `obj_size` returns NULL having spent no `rb_malloc` call at all. `pool_stats` is three maintained counters (one of them the sum `free_count + carve_remaining`) and is O(1). `pool_destroy` walks the slab chain saving `slab->next` before each `rb_free`, then releases the pool struct. A pool built by this slice owns no slabs and can hand nothing out: `live` is always 0 and the invariant always reads `0 + 0 == 0 * objs_per_slab`.
PLANNED, NOT IMPLEMENTED (and deliberately absent from this commit): `pool_alloc`, `pool_free`, slab growth, slot carving, the intrusive free list, 0xDD debug poisoning, the bounded debug cross-check walk that will keep `free_count` honest, and `rb_create_pooled`. Two fields (`carve_next`, `free_head`) are written by `pool_create` and read by nothing yet, and two more (`free_count`, `carve_remaining`) are read only inside the `pool_stats` sum, where both are permanently zero — the whole struct went in at once so later slices add behavior without churning the layout, and the comments name which slice claims each field. `pool_destroy`'s chain walk — the save-`next`-before-`rb_free` rule that is the entire point of the function — is therefore written but unexercised until slabs exist in slice B.
DID: implemented the three functions in `src/pool.c`; added five scenarios plus `check_pool_invariant()` and `pool_capacity()` to `tests/test_rbtree.c` (31 pool assertions, 805 total in the unit binary). The decisive argument was not the saved allocation but that eager buys nothing: the "no capacity, grow" branch `pool_alloc` needs for slab 2 is the same branch it needs for slab 1, so eager would have added a second failure path and a real unwind to `pool_create` in exchange for one fewer execution of a branch that has to exist anyway. question. The same pass also noted that nothing in the design needs the object-to-slab mapping
anyway: a single intrusive free list makes `pool_free` indifferent to which slab an object came
from, which is what keeps it O(1).

**Rejected: the `src/pool.h` I was offered.** Claude's implementation plan proposed a new
`src/pool.h` to hold the geometry type and prototype (and, later, the §8.2 pool API), flagging it
as a decision for me because the spec's file tree names only `src/pool.c`. I rejected it: the
file-level map is fixed, and the repo already had the `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` precedent for test-only
visibility into internals (`rb_test_force_root_red` and friends), so the type and helper stay
inside `src/pool.c` and `tests/test_rbtree.c` declares the helper itself. I added the constraint
that drove the rest of the shape: the non-test build has to stay clean under `-Wall -Wextra
-Werror` even though no `pool_create` calls the helper yet, and **not** by broadening
`RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` globally or adding build machinery. That forced out two consequences — the
helper gets external linkage rather than `static` (a `static` unused function is a

results come back through out-parameters rather than a shared struct, since with no header a
struct would have to be duplicated in the test file. Claude compiled `pool.c` both ways
separately to confirm, rather than asserting it.

**Two tightenings of the test I specified myself.** First, the minimality assertion: Claude's plan
had `stride < obj_size + ALIGN`, which overflows for sizes near `SIZE_MAX` and measures against
the wrong baseline for objects smaller than a pointer. I replaced it with `effective_min =
max(obj_size, sizeof(void *))`, `stride >= effective_min`, `stride - effective_min < ALIGN`.
Second, I pinned the degenerate-size contract as *internal* only — zero size false, no-complete-
slot false, overflow detected before the arithmetic wraps, outputs zeroed on false — explicitly
refusing to let it become a public `pool_create` contract tonight, because that is a later design
decision and writing it down early would have quietly made it one.

M2: pooled node storage - rb_create_pooled, node_alloc/node_release

Wires src/pool.c underneath the tree's node allocation. struct rbtree
gains one field, rb_pool_t *pool, and NULL is the mode discriminator --
no flag, no second struct.

All mode-dependent decisions are confined to three places:
  - node_alloc/node_release, the single point where node storage is
    obtained and returned, which keeps rb_insert/rb_delete free of
    allocator branches;
  - rb_create_pooled, two fallible steps ordered handle-then-pool so
    there is exactly one thing to unwind (pool_create is itself
    all-or-nothing, so no goto-cleanup ladder is warranted);
  - rb_destroy's teardown.

Only NODE storage is pooled. Key copies are variable-length and stay on
the rb_malloc/rb_free seam.

Teardown: pooled nodes are NOT individually pool_free'd. Whole-tree
destruction is what pool_destroy is for -- it releases every slab
whether its slots were live, free-listed or never carved -- so per-node
pool_free would be an O(1)-per-node poisoning and free-list churn to
hand slots back to a pool about to cease existing. The walk is still
required for payloads: keys and values live outside the slabs, so each
must be freed while its node is still readable. Hence capture next,
free key, call value_free, (ordinary only) rb_free the node; then
pool_destroy, then the handle. Capturing next first matters more under
the pool, since a pooled node is still live slab memory afterwards and
a stale read would be invisible to ASan rather than reported.

rb_insert's key-copy failure path returns the slot via node_release, so
live + free_objs == slabs * objs_per_slab holds across the failure and
the caller keeps ownership of value.

include/rbtree.h untouched. No src/pool.h -- the spec's file map is
fixed, so the pool entry points are declared extern here with
rb_pool_t left incomplete, as tests/test_rbtree.c already does.

Verified green at this state (before the test-side changes that follow):
make test, make asan, make memcheck all clean from a clean rebuild.

mode_label that check() prefixes, so a failure names the mode it failed
in. 29 of 32 rb_create sites now call make_tree; main() runs
run_tree_suite() once per mode. Nothing is duplicated and no assertion
is weakened to accommodate the second pass.

Three fault tests deliberately keep naming rb_create: arm(1/2/3) pins
src/rbtree.c's own ordinals (handle, node struct, key copy), which
under the pool are different allocations in different numbers -- a
pooled run of them would not be the same claim. Pool-internal tests
(geometry, pool_create/alloc/free/destroy) are not tree tests and stay
outside the two-mode suite.

The sweep stays the natural n = 1, 2, 3, ... loop: same assertions,
same termination condition (fault_alloc_total() < n). Only its
creation-failure message changed, because pooled creation spans two
allocations so n == 1 and n == 2 both land there via different unwind
paths. overwrite/delete-allocate-nothing join the two-mode suite
because those claims hold of rb_malloc and pool_free alike.

New pooled targeted tests for the claims the heap path cannot make:
both creation unwind paths, slab-purchase failure, and key-copy failure
-- the last asserting the follow-up insert costs exactly one rb_malloc,
which can only hold if the rolled-back slot went back to the pool
rather than being stranded.

tests/fuzz.c: usage is now `fuzz <ops> [seed|-] [heap|pooled]`; "-"
keeps time(NULL) seeding so both passes keep exploring new op streams.
Makefile runs the fuzzer at the full 100000 in both modes under test
and 20000 in both under valgrind -- op counts unreduced.

Battery, clean rebuild each time: make test 1897 assertions 0 failures
and both fuzz modes OK; make asan (address+undefined) clean in both
modes; make memcheck 3 x "no leaks are possible", 3 x 0 errors.

excluded is identical -- all 565 non-sweep tree assertions ran in both
modes, same order -- so nothing degraded into a no-op. The delta is
sweep arithmetic: heap allocates 1 + 3*2 = 7 and terminates at n = 8,
pooled allocates 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6 and terminates at n = 7; the five
remaining lines are make_int's fixture check firing from inside the
sweep (hand-derived: 16 heap vs 11 pooled).

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project status

This is a CS370 lab implementing a red-black tree in C, now on its second assignment (HW2,
`CS370-HW2.pdf`, a continuation of HW1). `include/rbtree.h` is the frozen contract — it was
re-frozen for HW2 and now also declares `rb_create_pooled` (Mutation 2: node storage drawn
from an internal slab pool) and `rb_snapshot` (Mutation 4: O(1) copy-on-write snapshot, "The
Reach" — no longer just ungraded prep, see below). Neither is implemented yet. `NOTES.md`
contains the assignment spec, the design decisions already made (including a devlog of the
NIL/parent-pointer/teardown reasoning and an HW2 section with spec notes/tips), and
constraints that must not be violated — read it before writing any code here.

Current state of `src/rbtree.c`: `rb_create`, the node/tree structs (with parent pointer),
the `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` seam, `rb_find` (real BST search), `rb_size`, `rb_insert` (with
rotations and insertion fixup, all cases + mirrors), `rb_foreach` (recursive in-order),
`rb_validate` (all five invariants), and `rb_destroy` are implemented. `rb_destroy` already
uses the non-recursive "Reach" technique (rotate into a right spine while freeing) — see
"The Reach" below; it is not just the ungraded future work it's described as there.
**`rb_delete` is now implemented**, including `delete_fixup` (the doubly-black fixup loop,
all cases plus the mirrored right-child symmetry) — both live in `src/rbtree.c` as of the
M2 commits (`f32e9ef`..`8c55919`). `tests/fault_alloc.c` is implemented as of HW2's M1
commits (`a250531`, `a8f4439`). `src/pool.c` now holds the Mutation 2 slot-geometry helper
only — the pool's allocation/carving/free-list machinery and `rb_create_pooled` are still
out of scope until their respective slices.

`tests/fuzz.c` runs insert/find/delete ops against a reference-model oracle (an array of
key/value pairs), interleaving `rb_delete` per its later M2 commit. `tests/test_rbtree.c`
...[57-80]...
work (pool allocator, fault injection, snapshot/Reach) starts from here and must not regress
it.

## Code map

- `include/rbtree.h` — frozen public API / graded contract. Never edit.
- `src/rbtree.c` — tree logic: allocation/ownership, rotations, insertion and deletion
  fixups, `rb_validate`, teardown. All heap allocation here goes through the `rb_malloc`/
  `rb_free` seam.
- `src/pool.c` — HW2 slab pool implementation (backs `rb_create_pooled`). Currently the slot
  geometry only: `rb_pool_geometry` (stride, first-slot offset, slots per slab, tail slack)
  plus the in-band `struct rb_slab` header whose size it accounts for. Internal to the file by
  design — no `src/pool.h`, since the spec's file map is fixed; `tests/test_rbtree.c` declares
  the helper itself under `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS`, as it already does for the `rb_test_*` hooks.
- `tests/test_rbtree.c` — unit tests / HW1 regression suite (table-driven `rb_delete` cases,
  insertion-fixup cases, validate, destroy, overwrite semantics).
- `tests/fuzz.c` — randomized stress driver / reference-model (oracle) testing against a
  plain array of key/value pairs.
- `tests/fault_alloc.c` / `tests/fault_alloc.h` — allocation-seam shim and fault-injection
  support for HW2 (make allocation fail on demand). Implemented: `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` plus
  `fault_alloc_arm`/`fault_alloc_disarm`/`fault_alloc_total`.

- `src/rbtree.c` — tree logic: allocation/ownership, rotations, insertion and deletion
  fixups, `rb_validate`, teardown. All heap allocation here goes through the `rb_malloc`/
  `rb_free` seam.
- `src/pool.c` — HW2 slab pool implementation (backs `rb_create_pooled`). Currently the slot
  geometry only: `rb_pool_geometry` (stride, first-slot offset, slots per slab, tail slack)
  plus the in-band `struct rb_slab` header whose size it accounts for. Internal to the file by
  design — no `src/pool.h`, since the spec's file map is fixed; `tests/test_rbtree.c` declares
  the helper itself under `RBTREE_TEST_HOOKS`, as it already does for the `rb_test_*` hooks.
- `tests/test_rbtree.c` — unit tests / HW1 regression suite (table-driven `rb_delete` cases,
  insertion-fixup cases, validate, destroy, overwrite semantics).
- `tests/fuzz.c` — randomized stress driver / reference-model (oracle) testing against a
  plain array of key/value pairs.
- `tests/fault_alloc.c` / `tests/fault_alloc.h` — allocation-seam shim and fault-injection
  support for HW2 (make allocation fail on demand). Implemented: `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` plus
  `fault_alloc_arm`/`fault_alloc_disarm`/`fault_alloc_total`.

Before committing slice 1 I also wrote a throwaway scratch driver (never added to the repo) to exercise the pooled path, since the repo's own suite did not reach it yet.
DECIDED: (1) **`NULL` is the mode discriminator** — one `rb_pool_t *pool` field, no enum, no flag, no second struct — and every mode-dependent decision is confined to `node_alloc`/`node_release`, `rb_create_pooled`, and `rb_destroy`'s teardown branch, so `rb_insert` and `rb_delete` grew no allocator branches at all. (2) **Allocation order in `rb_create_pooled` is handle-then-pool**, which leaves exactly one thing to unwind; since `pool_create` validates geometry before its single `rb_malloc` and is therefore all-or-nothing, there is never a half-built pool and no goto-cleanup ladder is warranted. (3) **Pooled teardown does not `pool_free` each node** — this reversed my own proposal, which had the walk drive `live` to zero so teardown could assert it. Whole-tree destruction is exactly what `pool_destroy` is for, and the per-node pass would have been poisoning and free-list churn to hand slots back to a pool about to cease existing; the walk survives only because keys and values live *outside* the slabs. (4) **The fault sweep stays the natural `n = 1, 2, 3, …` loop**, not a discover-then-arm rewrite: its structure (arm `n`, assert the failure landed at call `n`, terminate when `total < n`) is already mode-agnostic, and only its creation-failure *message* needed changing because pooled creation spans two allocations. NEXT FIRST STEP: Mutation 3 — the non-recursive O(1)-auxiliary-space `rb_foreach` (currently recursive, which HW1 §9 permitted and HW2 does not), and the million-node teardown case, which per NOTES.md belongs behind its own target so `make memcheck` still finishes; run the large case under ASan and a smaller one under valgrind, and say so in REFLECTION.md rather than quietly shrinking it.
OPEN: `rb_snapshot` (Mutation 4) and Mutation 3's `rb_foreach` are the only unimplemented pieces of the frozen header. The tree-driven pool invariant is deliberately unchecked (see DECIDED 6) and should be revisited if the existing tests ever prove insufficient. `make memcheck` still does not depend on `clean`, so the ASan-binary staleness trap recorded on 2026-10-07 and 2026-10-08 remains live and a false green from it is still a real risk — unresolved for the third session running, and worth just fixing. Procedural gap: slices B and C (`0ebee46`, `21a44be`) have no DEVLOG entries of their own — tonight's entry does not substitute for them.
EOF

(3) **Pooled teardown does not `pool_free` each node** — this reversed my own proposal, which had the walk drive `live` to zero so teardown could assert it. (7) **Op counts unreduced** — the fuzzer runs the full 10^5 in both modes under `test`/`asan` and 2×10^4 in both under valgrind, accepting a third valgrind invocation rather than trimming to protect runtime.

There is a real false-green risk in the current Makefile:
after `make asan`, `make memcheck` can reuse the ASan-built binaries and Valgrind

Fix only that.

Requirements:

- Keep the existing heap + pooled Valgrind runs and their current op counts.
- Do not change compiler requirements or weaken any tests.
- Do not touch source code, tests, CLAUDE.md, DEVLOG.md, PROMPTLOG.md, or NOTES.md.
- Keep the Makefile change minimal.

Important: do not implement this as `memcheck: clean all` if that could allow
parallel prerequisite execution to violate the required clean-then-build order.
Prefer an explicitly ordered recipe, e.g. `memcheck: clean` followed by
`$(MAKE) all` before the Valgrind commands.

Then verify specifically with:
1. make asan
2. make memcheck

Show the relevant output proving Valgrind sees real allocations rather than
0 allocs / 0 frees.

If green, show the diff and stop before committing.

Also correct one documentation claim from your prior report:
the HW2 spec requires 6-10 PROMPTLOG episodes, not 4-6. We currently have 8,
which is within spec. Do not trim them.

python3 - <<'PY'
p='Makefile'
s=open(p).read()
old='''memcheck: all
	valgrind'''
assert s.count(old)==1
new='''# memcheck depends on `clean` ALONE and then builds via a recursive $(MAKE)
# in the recipe, rather than `memcheck: clean all`. Two reasons, both real:
# with `clean all` as sibling prerequisites, -j is free to run them
# concurrently and `clean` can delete build/ after `all` populated it (or
# race it mid-compile); and even serially, make decides `all` is up to date
# based on the binaries present when it builds its graph. After `make asan`
# those binaries exist and are ASan-instrumented, so valgrind would run
# against them -- which reports "0 allocs, 0 frees" and "no leaks are
# possible" over a binary whose allocator it cannot see, i.e. a gate that
# passes having tested nothing. One prerequisite plus an ordered recipe makes
# clean-then-build the only possible sequence at any -j.
memcheck: clean
	$(MAKE) all
	valgrind'''
s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("ok")
PY
echo "=== 1. make asan ===" && make asan 2>&1 | grep -E "^FAIL|All tests passed|ops OK"; echo "asan EXIT=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

Green, uncommitted, `Makefile` only — one target line plus its comment. Nothing else touched.

## Proof

**Before the fix** (`make asan`, then `make memcheck` with no manual clean):

```
==240319==ASan runtime does not come first in initial library list...
==240319==   total heap usage: 0 allocs, 0 frees, 0 bytes allocated

==240319== ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors from 0 contexts
```

**After the fix** — same sequence, no manual clean:

```
rm -rf build
make all
gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude -Itests -DRBTREE_TEST_HOOKS ... -o build/test_rbtree
gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude -Itests ... -o build/fuzz

All tests passed.

==240738== ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors from 0 contexts
fuzz: heap: 20000 ops OK
==240739==   total heap usage: 20,043 allocs, 20,043 frees, 465,896 bytes allocated
==240739== ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors from 0 contexts
fuzz: pooled: 20000 ops OK
==240773==   total heap usage: 15,881 allocs, 15,881 frees, 366,936 bytes allocated
==240773== ERROR SUMMARY: 0 errors from 0 contexts
memcheck EXIT=0
```

Real allocations on all three runs, no `-fsanitize` in the recompile, no ASan-runtime warning, both heap and pooled valgrind runs kept at 20000 ops. `make asan` is unchanged and still green (100000 ops, both modes).

A detail worth noting as independent corroboration: pooled fuzz shows **15,881** allocations against heap's **20,043** on the same workload. That gap is the pool doing its job — node storage coming from slabs instead of one `malloc` per node — so these numbers also confirm the pooled run genuinely exercised the pool rather than quietly falling through to `rb_malloc`.

Ordering verified under `make -j8 memcheck` after `make asan`: `rm -rf build` → `make all` → real allocations, exit 0. Single prerequisite plus an ordered recipe, so no sibling-parallelism window exists.

## Two things to flag

**1. The pre-fix failure was loud here, not silent.** On this machine the unfixed `make memcheck` exited **2**, because the ASan-runtime complaint aborted the binary before `main`. So I should sharpen what I told you earlier: the false green is environment-dependent, not guaranteed. What *is* guaranteed and was wrong in every case is that `make memcheck` after `make asan` tested nothing — note `All tests passed` never appeared in the pre-fix output, and the `0 allocs / 0 frees` + `0 errors` + `--error-exitcode=1` combination is precisely the shape that passes silently wherever the abort doesn't happen. The fix is right either way; my "false green" framing was the risk, and here the observed symptom was a hard failure.

**2. `asan: clean test` has the identical sibling-prerequisite shape** and I left it alone per your scope. I probed it: `make -j8 asan` passed 3/3 with both files compiled instrumented. That is not a guarantee — make is free to run `clean` and `test` concurrently there, it just happened to serialize. Lower stakes than the memcheck case (a race yields a build error or a missing binary, not a gate that passes having tested nothing), but it's the same latent bug and a one-line change of the same form whenever you want it.

## Correction

You're right, and my earlier report was wrong: the spec requires **6–10** PROMPTLOG episodes, not 4–6. Eight is comfortably within spec and nothing should be trimmed.

That figure came from `CLAUDE.md:173`, which states 4–6 — so the error is recorded in the repo, not just in my report, and it propagated: the preamble note I committed to `PROMPTLOG.md` in `2dc65e3` cites 4–6 and names Episodes 3 and 5 as cut candidates. Both files are on your do-not-touch list for this task, so I've changed neither. Two stale claims to clear when you're ready:

- `CLAUDE.md:173` — "4–6 annotated episodes" → 6–10
- `PROMPTLOG.md` preamble — drop the overage note entirely; 8 is in range, so there is nothing to justify

Say the word and I'll fix both in a separate commit. Stopping here as asked — the Makefile change is unstaged.

build: serialize sanitizer and memcheck rebuilds

Both gates rebuilt from scratch via sibling prerequisites (asan: clean
test, memcheck: all), which make does not order. Two failure modes:
-j is free to run clean concurrently with the build, so clean can
delete build/ after it was populated or race it mid-compile; and even
serially, make decides whether test/all is up to date from the binaries
present when it builds its graph, which right after a make asan are the
ASan-instrumented ones.

For memcheck that produced a gate that passed having tested nothing.
Valgrind over an ASan-built binary reports "0 allocs, 0 frees" and "All
heap blocks were freed -- no leaks are possible", so --error-exitcode=1
never fires. Observed before this change, running memcheck straight
after asan: 0 allocs, 0 frees, 0 errors, and the unit binary never ran
at all. (On this machine the ASan runtime complaint also aborted the
process, so it failed loudly here rather than silently -- but the
silent shape is what the recipe permits, and either way the valgrind
gate covered nothing.)

Both targets now take clean as their sole prerequisite and drive the
build from an ordered recipe, so clean-then-build is the only possible
sequence at any -j. asan passes its effective CFLAGS to the sub-make as
a command-line assignment: the target-specific += is in scope inside
asan's own recipe, but the sub-make never visits the asan target, so
without passing it the sanitizer flags would be silently lost.
TEST_CFLAGS stays recursively expanded so the hooks build picks them up
too.

Coverage and op counts unchanged: asan still runs the full test target
(unit suite plus 100000 fuzz ops in each of heap and pooled), memcheck
still runs the unit binary plus 20000 ops in each mode under valgrind.

Verified at -j8, three consecutive asan -> memcheck cycles, identical
each time:

    sanitizer flags; valgrind reports real allocation counts --

The pooled fuzz run allocating measurably less than heap on the same
workload is the pool doing its job, and is corroboration that the
pooled pass used it rather than falling through to rb_malloc.

Both commits in, working tree clean. Stopping here — no Mutation 3 work.

## `bdbb900 build: serialize sanitizer and memcheck rebuilds`

`Makefile` only, 28 insertions / 2 deletions — most of it the comment explaining why.

```make
asan: CFLAGS += -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer
asan: clean
	$(MAKE) test CFLAGS="$(CFLAGS)"

memcheck: clean
	$(MAKE) all
	valgrind ...
```

Each target takes `clean` as its **sole** prerequisite and drives the build from an ordered recipe, so there is no sibling-parallelism window at any `-j`.

On the CFLAGS concern you flagged — it was real and worth calling out. The target-specific `+=` is in scope inside `asan`'s own recipe, so `$(CFLAGS)` there is already augmented; but the sub-make never visits the `asan` target, so without passing it explicitly the sanitizer flags would have been **silently** lost — a green `make asan` testing an uninstrumented build. The command-line assignment carries it across, and `TEST_CFLAGS` being recursively expanded (`=`) means the `-DRBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` build picks it up too.

### Verification (all four, at `-j8`)

| # | check | result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `make -j8 asan` | exit 0; `All tests passed`; both fuzz modes OK at 100000 |
| 2 | `make -j8 memcheck` straight after | exit 0 |
| 3 | asan compiles carry `-fsanitize=address,undefined` | **both** binaries, including the `-DRBTREE_TEST_HOOKS` one |
| 4 | memcheck recompiles clean, real allocations | no `-fsanitize` in either compile; `1,102/1,102` unit, `19,991/19,991` fuzz heap, `15,588/15,588` fuzz pooled; 0 errors on all three |

Three consecutive `asan` → `memcheck` cycles at `-j8` were byte-identical in outcome: 2 instrumented binaries each time, 0 sanitizer flags in the memcheck build, 0 zero-alloc runs, 3 nonzero-alloc runs. Coverage and op counts are unchanged — asan still runs the full `test` target (unit suite + 100000 ops × 2 modes), memcheck still 20000 ops × 2 modes.

Worth keeping: pooled fuzz allocates measurably less than heap on the same workload (15,588 vs 19,991), which is the pool working and independent corroboration that the pooled pass actually used it rather than falling through to `rb_malloc`.

## `8cd7c72 docs: correct PROMPTLOG episode requirement`

- `CLAUDE.md:234` — 4–6 → **6–10**
- `PROMPTLOG.md` — the overage note removed, 4 lines gone

Verified nothing else moved: the diff is a single contiguous deletion in the preamble, all 8 episode headers unchanged in text and order, numbering untouched, and the preamble's commit list and span left as they were.

Two notes on this:

1. The error originated in `CLAUDE.md`, not in my report — I read 4–6 from the repo and propagated it into `PROMPTLOG.md` in `2dc65e3` without checking it against the PDF. Since `CLAUDE.md` is the file I'm instructed to treat as authoritative, the practical lesson is that its process-requirements section is worth spot-checking against the spec rather than trusting; I can't read the PDFs directly in this environment (no `pdftotext` or `pypdf` available), so a numeric requirement there is only as good as whoever last transcribed it.
2. The wrong figure is now corrected in the working tree but still present in the history of `2dc65e3`. That's correct behavior for a devlog-style repo and nothing to fix, but if a grader reads commit bodies you may want to know it's there.

Mutation 3 remains untouched: `rb_snapshot` and the non-recursive O(1)-auxiliary-space `rb_foreach` are still the only unimplemented pieces of the frozen header.
